segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I praise you because you remember me in everything and hold fast to the traditions just as I handed them on to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every man who prays or prophesies with something on his head shames his head;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered shames her head, for it is one and the same thing as having her head shaved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if a woman does not cover herself, let her also have her hair cut off. But if it is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut off or to be shaved, let her cover herself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For man is not from woman, but woman from man;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and man was not created for the sake of the woman, but woman for the sake of the man.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not apart from man, nor man apart from woman.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; and all things are from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a woman to pray to God uncovered?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair has been given as a covering.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the assemblies of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In giving this instruction, however, I do not praise you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For, in the first place, when you come together as an assembly, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there must indeed be factions among you, so that those who are approved may become evident among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when you come together in one place, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for when it comes to eating, each of you goes ahead with your own supper, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you really not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the assembly of God and shame those who have nothing? What should I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night he was handed over, took bread,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each person should examine themselves, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whoever eats and drinks without judging the body rightly eats and drinks judgment on themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if we judged ourselves rightly, we would not be judged.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone is hungry, they should eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment. The rest I will set in order when I come.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for the head of the body, and its figurative force here is long disputed. Most lexical studies favor a sense of authority or preeminence; others argue for “source,” pointing to verses 8 and 12, where woman is “from” man. The translation keeps “head” because Paul plays on the literal and figurative senses through verse 10, so that “shames his head” in verse 4 can mean his own head, Christ, or both.

notes.phrase: the head of a woman is the man
notes.traditional: the head of the woman is the man
notes.note: Greek uses one word for “man” and “husband” and one for “woman” and “wife.” Some versions render “the head of a wife is her husband” and read the passage as concerning married couples. The translation keeps “man” and “woman” throughout because verses 8–9 and 12 argue from creation and birth, but the marital sense may be in view in places.

The Greek is literally “having down from the head.” Most interpreters take it as a covering hanging over the head, such as the fold of a garment that Roman men drew up when offering sacrifice. Some take it instead as long hair hanging down, in line with verse 14.

notes.traditional: have a symbol of authority on her head
notes.note: Many versions supply “a symbol of” and take the phrase to mean a covering that marks the woman as under authority; those words are not in the Greek. Elsewhere the idiom “to have authority over” something means to have control of it, and it is rendered that way here: she is to exercise control over her head, presumably by keeping it covered. The traditional reading remains possible, and the verse is among the most disputed in the letter.

Paul does not explain this phrase. The most common proposal is that angels were thought to be present when the community worshiped and to care for its good order; another links it to the tradition, based on Genesis 6, of angels who desired human women. No explanation commands general agreement.

The preposition most often means “in place of,” which would make long hair itself the woman’s covering. It can also mean “as” or “answering to,” so that her hair is nature’s counterpart to the covering Paul asks for. Because verses 5–6 distinguish being uncovered from being shorn, most interpreters take it the second way, and the rendering leaves that open.

The traditional rendering is “church.” A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and, from the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God; “church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” is near-universal in English versions and readers know what it refers to, but this translation uses “assembly” everywhere so that the one Greek word stays visible.

The verb can mean “take beforehand,” implying that some began their meal before others, perhaps the poorer members, had arrived; it can also mean simply “consume,” with no idea of time. The matching instruction in verse 33 has the same ambiguity: “wait for one another” could also be “welcome one another.” The translation follows the temporal reading, which is the more common one.

Most versions have “on the night he was betrayed.” The verb is the ordinary word for handing a person or thing into another’s control, and it is the same verb translated “handed on” earlier in this verse and in verse 2. “Betrayed” narrows the reference to Judas; “handed over” leaves room for the wider chain in which Jesus is handed over by Judas, by the authorities, and, in Paul’s own usage elsewhere, by God. Many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context and not the word’s meaning, though others defend it here.

Many later manuscripts read “which is broken for you,” and that form passed into the King James Version and much liturgy; a few read “given.” Later manuscripts also add “Take, eat” before the saying. The earliest witnesses have only “which is for you,” and the longer forms are generally regarded as expansions.

The traditional rendering is “discerning the body.” The verb is a compound of “judge,” and in verses 29–32 Paul strings together a chain of related words (judgment, judge rightly, judged, condemned); the rendering keeps that chain audible. What “the body” means is disputed: the Lord’s body represented in the bread, or the gathered community as Christ’s body, whose poorer members were being shamed. Some later manuscripts add “unworthily” and “of the Lord.”

Sleep was a common euphemism for death, in Greek generally and especially among early Christians. Paul means that a number of the community have died, and he connects this with the abuses at the supper.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Hebrews, where translators vary between “covenant,” “testament” and “will,” and the reader should see one word unless the legal sense is clearly meant.
The plural address occurs throughout the letters and versions split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “friends”; it needs one policy.
The choice between “woman” and “wife” (and “man” and “husband” for ἀνήρ) affects several disputed passages and should be made by a consistent rule.
Versions vary between “judgment,” “condemnation” and “damnation,” and the distinction from κατάκριμα and κρίσις needs to be held consistently.
The verb and its cognates (δόκιμος, ἀδόκιμος, δοκιμή) range over “test,” “examine,” “approve” and “prove,” and their link is lost when the English varies freely.
